text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Sweden's minority Social Democratic government will forecast unemployment of 4.5 percent at the turn of the century in its spring budget proposal on Tuesday. Thereby the government will not reach its target to halve unemployment to four percent by 2000.

- Swedish investment company Investor, the key holding company in the Wallenberg family's financial empire, will increase its stake in S-E-Banken, family head Peter Wallenberg told the newspaper. Investor has already boosted its S-E-Banken holding to 9.6 percent of votes and 9.2 percent of capital.
- Construction company Skanska will sell all of its shares in tool and engineering group Sandvik for around 10 billion crowns.

- Construction company Skanska will sell its Sandvik stake, worth 10 billion crowns, pocketing a capital gain of around nine billion crowns. Skanska chairman Percy Barnevik, who will step down to take the chair in investment company Investor, has had difficulty finding an industrial buyer so four billion crowns worth of Sandvik shares will be sold to investment company Industrivarden.

- A 16 billion crown expansion programme for 1998 is the core of the minority Social Democratic government's spring budget proposal. The program encompasses health care, elderly care, schools, other education, growth, companies and labour market policies. In addition, the government promises easings for companies and households in 1999.

- German electricity group Hamburgische Electricitaets-Werke AG (HEW) bought a 5.1 billion crown stake in Swedish power company Sydkraft on Monday. Thereby German nuclear power could, via the Baltic Cable, replace Sydkraft's nuclear power plant Barseback which the government has decided to close.

- Construction giant Skanska should make more than nine billion crowns capital gain when it divests it entire holding in Sandvik, the tools and speciality steel company. The divestment is part of the back to basics strategy that has led to the sale of the company's non-core businesses. The company has also changed its executive management and board and proposes to distribute some of its cash holding to shareholders through an eight-10 billion crowns share redemption.

- The German power utility Hamburger Elektricitats-Werke has paid a 17 percent premium to acquire shares corresponding to 15.7 percent of the capital stock in Sydkraft, Sweden's second largest power utility. For its part Sydkraft has been building a stake in HEW since early 1997 and now owns 13.3 percent of the German company's capital.
- Ikea, the Swedish home interior retailer, is moving into the capital markets with mutual funds. Catella, a company in the Ikea business sphere, will handle sales of the funds.
